intro: Frank Lévy plays Chopin’s Second Ballade, which pairs an F-major song, marked Andantino, with an A-minor Presto con fuoco. Chopin finished the work during his winter on Mallorca.

sections.label: A · Andantino song in F major
sections.mNote: Repeated Cs open a rocking melody.

sections.label: B · A minor, Presto con fuoco
sections.mNote: Rapid figures in A minor cut off the Andantino theme

sections.label: A′ · F-major melody returns, enlarged
sections.mNote: The F-major melody returns with new harmonies.

sections.label: B′ · Presto con fuoco in A minor returns
sections.mNote: The fast figures return and lead into the coda.

sections.label: Coda · Agitato in A minor
sections.mNote: A new closing theme leads to the final cadence

sections.label: A″ · Opening theme in A minor
sections.mNote: The opening melody returns pianissimo in the Presto’s key.

cues.title: Opening theme in F major
cues.text: The Ballade begins with repeated Cs in both hands. A melody in F major grows out of them, marked sotto voce, under the breath. The metre is six quavers to the bar, and the piano plays the melody in chords.
cues.evidence: Opening notes, sotto voce and 6/8 metre: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._2_(Chopin). Mieczysław Tomaszewski describes the opening siciliana at https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Schumann’s diary, October 1840
cues.text: In October 1840 Schumann noted that Chopin’s new Ballade was dedicated to him. “It gives me greater joy than if I’d received an order from some ruler,” he wrote in his diary.
cues.evidence: Schumann’s diary, October 1840, quoted by Mieczysław Tomaszewski for the Fryderyk Chopin Institute. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96

cues.title: Presto con fuoco in A minor
cues.text: The opening song gives way to Presto con fuoco. The piano plays rapid figures with heavy accents, in A minor. Chopin sets the two tempos and the two keys against each other.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski, Fryderyk Chopin Institute: the contrasting A-minor Presto and its interruption of the F-major siciliana. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the Andantino
cues.text: The Andantino returns with its melody in F major and its rocking chords. The continuation grows stronger and moves through new harmonies.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski describes the returning siciliana’s growth in strength and its transformation. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Julian Fontana, January 1839
cues.text: In January 1839 a Pleyel piano reached Chopin on Mallorca. He wrote to Julian Fontana in Paris: “You’ll soon receive the Preludes and the Ballade.” He was then working on the music in the former monastery at Valldemossa.
cues.evidence: Chopin to Julian Fontana, January 1839, quoted with the Pleyel’s arrival and Mallorca setting by Tomaszewski. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96

cues.title: Schumann’s review, 1840
cues.text: Reviewing the Ballade in 1840, Schumann recalled Chopin playing it in Leipzig four years earlier: “It ended in F major; now it closes in A minor.” By Schumann’s account, the fiery episodes were later additions.
cues.evidence: Schumann, Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1840; quoted in Tomaszewski’s commentary. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96

cues.title: Return of the Presto
cues.text: The Presto returns in A minor. This time the fast music continues, and its figures are extended towards a new closing theme.
cues.evidence: The renewed Presto and concluding theme are described by Tomaszewski. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Coda, Agitato
cues.text: The coda is marked Agitato. A new theme drives the fast music to its cadence in A minor. After it the piano plays one short pianissimo phrase.
cues.evidence: Chopin, Ballade Op. 38, closing Agitato; Tomaszewski describes the new final theme and the subsequent pianissimo recollection. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening theme
cues.text: A fragment of the opening song returns pianissimo, now in A minor, the key of the Presto. The Ballade ends on these few notes in A minor.
cues.evidence: Tomaszewski identifies the final siciliana fragment, its pianissimo marking and A-minor harmony. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A minor interrupts F major
transitions.from: A · Andantino song in F major
transitions.to: B · A minor, Presto con fuoco
transitions.how: The F-major Andantino closes on repeated As in the right hand. These notes become the tonic of the A-minor Presto con fuoco. The piano moves straight into rapid figures with forceful accents, and the tempo changes without a connecting passage.
transitions.evidence: Repeated As before the Presto: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballade_No._2_(Chopin). Tonal contrast and tempo: https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96.

transitions.title: Return of the F-major Andantino
transitions.from: B · A minor, Presto con fuoco
transitions.how: The fast A-minor figures die away. At the return of the Andantino, the piano takes up the F-major song again, with its rocking chordal accompaniment. The melody begins softly and then extends into a newly written continuation.
transitions.evidence: Tomaszewski’s account of the returning and transformed siciliana. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96

transitions.title: Return of the A-minor Presto
transitions.to: B′ · Presto con fuoco in A minor returns
transitions.how: The song’s expanded continuation leads back to Presto con fuoco. A minor and the rapid piano figures return together. This second fast span is longer than the earlier interruption and continues into the coda.
transitions.evidence: Tomaszewski, on the collision of the themes and the final theme that follows. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96

transitions.title: Agitato continues in A minor
transitions.from: B′ · Presto con fuoco in A minor returns
transitions.how: The fast piano writing continues into a new closing theme, marked Agitato. A minor holds through the coda. Short, urgent figures replace the long F-major song and press towards a cadence.
transitions.evidence: Chopin, Ballade Op. 38, closing Agitato; Tomaszewski’s account of its new final theme. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96

transitions.title: The opening melody returns in A minor
transitions.to: A″ · Opening theme in A minor
transitions.how: After the coda’s A-minor cadence, the piano recalls a fragment of the opening melody pianissimo. The slower rhythm of the opening returns, and the harmony stays in A minor.
transitions.evidence: Tomaszewski identifies the closing pianissimo recollection in A minor. https://chopin.nifc.pl/en/chopin/kompozycja/96

composer.born: 1 March 1810 by his family’s reckoning; the parish register gives 22 February, Żelazowa Wola, Duchy of Warsaw
composer.epithet: Composer for the piano, known for music that drew on operatic singing and on the irregular accents of the mazurka.
facts: Wojciech Żywny; composition with Józef Elsner in Warsaw, 1826–29
Warsaw · Paris from 1831 · summers at Nohant
Piano lessons, publishing and occasional concerts
The piano, from a few lines of mazurka to concertos and sonatas
composer.background:
In February 1832 Chopin, a twenty-one-year-old Polish pianist, played in the Pleyel rooms in Paris. He had arrived the previous autumn, with two concertos behind him. The concert caught the attention of the city’s publishers, and teaching soon supplied his living. For the rest of his life his profession depended on people hearing him at close quarters. The great public virtuosos travelled from one concert city to the next; Chopin stayed in Paris and gave lessons.

He was born at Żelazowa Wola in 1810. His father, Nicolas, had come from France and worked as a tutor; his mother, Justyna Krzyżanowska, was Polish. The family moved to Warsaw while Fryderyk was still a baby, when Nicolas obtained a teaching post at the Lyceum. At seven the boy had a polonaise in print. Wojciech Żywny taught him the piano, with Bach and Mozart among his models; Józef Elsner later gave him a rigorous training in composition at Warsaw’s Main School of Music.
